english: I will take my medicine before the meeting.
tip: 약을 먹다 (yageul meokda) — Korean "eats" all medicine, even syrup.

english: I will pop out to the pharmacy at lunchtime.
tip: 다녀오다 (danyeooda) = go and come back: 다녀올게요 = I'll be right back.

english: Don't push yourself — rest instead.
tip: -지 말고 (-ji malgo) = don't do A, do B instead: 무리하지 말고 쉬세요.

english: Where does it hurt (what brings you in)?
tip: Staff honor the customer: 오셨어요 (osyeosseoyo) = did you come + -시-.

english: Let me take your temperature.
tip: -아/어 볼게요 (bolgeyo) = I'll just try doing: 재 볼게요 = let me measure it.

english: It is a cold. Don't worry.
tip: -지 마세요 (-ji maseyo) = please don't: 걱정하지 마세요 = don't worry.

english: You will get an injection today.
tip: 주사를 맞다 (jusareul matda) = "receive" a shot — never 하다.

english: I will prescribe you some medicine.
tip: 드릴게요 (deurilgeyo) = I'll give — humble, done FOR the listener.

english: I had a toothache, so I went to the dentist.
tip: 치과 (chigwa) = dental clinic — -과 names the medical specialty.

english: What symptoms do you have?
tip: The pharmacist honors you: 있으세요 (isseuseyo) = honorific of 있어요.

english: Take it three times a day.
tip: 하루에 세 번 (harue se beon) = three times per day — 에 marks "per".

english: Take it after meals.
tip: 후 (hu) = after and 전 (jeon) = before attach straight to nouns: 식후에 (sikhue) = after meals. Same pair as in 오전/오후 (ojeon/ohu = a.m./p.m.).

target: 이 연고를 하루에 두 번 바르세요.
english: Apply this ointment twice a day.
tip: 바르다 (bareuda) = spread on — creams, ointment, sunscreen.

english: Do you have something for indigestion?
tip: 소화제 (sohwaje) = digestion aid; -제 = the medicine suffix.

english: I am a bit drowsy after taking the medicine.
tip: Korean splits tired: 졸려요 (jollyeoyo) = drowsy, ready to doze; 피곤해요 (pigonhaeyo) = worn out. Medicine makes you 졸려요 (jollyeoyo), the drowsy one.

english: You will be fine soon.
tip: Adjective + -아/어지다 = become: 괜찮아지다 (gwaenchanajida) = get better.

english: I am much better than yesterday.
tip: 보다 (boda) after a noun = than: 어제보다 = than yesterday.

english: Take good care of yourself.
tip: 몸조리 잘하세요 (momjori jalhaseyo) — the set phrase for "get well soon".

english: My grandmother has been unwell lately.
tip: Elders don't get plain 아프다 (apeuda = sick) – respect swaps in a whole different verb: 편찮으세요 (pyeonchaneuseyo) is how grandmother is unwell.

english: My grandfather's knees hurt.
tip: An elder's pain still takes -시-: 아프세요 (apeuseyo), not 아파요.

english: My parents are both healthy.
tip: 분 (bun) = honorific counter for people: 두 분 = two (respected) people.

english: I made rice porridge for my grandmother.
tip: 만들어 드렸어요 (mandeureo deuryeosseoyo) uses 드리다 (deurida), the humble 'give' for elders – with a friend the same favor would end in 줬어요 (jwosseoyo).

english: Colds are going around among the kids.
tip: 유행 (yuhaeng) = going around — fashion AND flu can both 유행이에요.

english: For preventing colds, hand-washing is key.
tip: -기 (-gi) makes a verb into a noun: 씻기 (ssitgi) = washing.

english: Exercise is good for your health.
tip: X에 좋아요 (e joayo) = good for X: 건강에 좋아요.

english: I got an upset stomach while traveling.
tip: 배탈이 나다 (baetari nada) = get a stomach bug — it "breaks out".

english: Please go with me to the hospital.
tip: -아/어 주세요 (juseyo) = do it for me: 가 주세요 = please go (with me).

english: The weather is really nice today, isn't it!
tip: -네요 (-neyo) = shared surprise: 좋네요 = it's nice, isn't it!

english: There was fog in the morning.
tip: 안개가 끼다 (angaega kkida) = fog "settles in": 안개가 꼈어요.

english: It is easy to catch a cold between seasons.
tip: -기 쉬워요 (-gi swiwoyo) = easy to do: 걸리기 쉬워요.
